comparison: Strong agreement on robustness claims (C57-C68, C98). Both evaluations find the extensive parameter exploration convincing, including different learning rules, noise types, and tasks. OpenEval notes specific caveats about label noise (C60) and speculative nature of C66, while peer reviewers emphasize the biological plausibility translation without questioning specific parameters.

Strong agreement on experimental data analysis (C8, C9, C38, C47-C56). Both find the evidence from four independent datasets convincing as corroboration of the model. OpenEval notes C48 is speculative about why other studies missed the effect, which peer reviewers also acknowledge by noting 'Future work should dig deeper.' Both accept the statistical significance (p < 0.011).

Strong agreement on the three-phase theoretical framework (C10, C69-C75). Both evaluations accept this as a key contribution. OpenEval notes C74 is speculative about why experiments missed phase 2, which aligns with peer reviewer acceptance of this as generating testable hypotheses. Both find the characterization of learning phases well-supported by data.

Strong agreement on sparsification phenomenon (C5, C6, C37, C41, C42, C44, C46). Both find the evidence from Figure 2C convincing, including timescale separation and increased spatial information while maintaining performance. Peer reviewers found evidence 'persuasive' and 'clearly demonstrate' the changes, matching OpenEval's 'well-documented' assessment.

Agreement on initial simulation setup and convergence (C3, C4, C35, C36, C40). Both evaluations accept these claims as supported by Figure 2B. OpenEval emphasizes consistency with prior work (Recanatesi et al., 2021), while peer reviewers incorporate these claims into their broader acceptance of the core finding.

Agreement on drift-like dynamics (C43, C45). Both evaluations accept the visual and quantitative evidence from Figures 2D and 2E showing consistency with experimental observations (Ziv et al., 2013). Peer reviewers found the overall demonstration 'clearly' showing these phenomena.

Strong agreement on biological plausibility arguments (C31-C34). Both evaluations accept these modeling assumptions without challenge. OpenEval finds the reasoning 'well-justified' with appropriate citations, while peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'make an important contribution by translating these findings into more biologically plausible models.'

Agreement on mechanistic connection between sparsification and Hessian structure (C79-C83). Both find the explanation clear and convincing. OpenEval notes the correlation is clearly shown and mathematical reasoning is sound, while peer reviewers state 'The mechanism underlying RD in these models is clearly laid out and the explanation given is convincing.'

Agreement on the 2D intuitive illustration (C76-C78). Both evaluations accept this as helpful for understanding the mechanism. OpenEval finds the mathematical explanation correct and intuition-building, while peer reviewers note the authors 'develop helpful intuition in Figure 5 by showing a minimal model that captures the essence of their result.'

Agreement on connection to ML theory (C7, C39). Both evaluations accept this interpretation as well-supported by the theoretical framework. OpenEval notes the mechanistic connection is further elaborated in later results, while peer reviewers accept the ML theory citations as 'convincing work.'

Agreement on theoretical foundation from ML literature (C27-C30). Both evaluations accept these theoretical results as providing sound foundation. OpenEval finds the description accurate, while peer reviewers state the authors 'cite convincing work from the machine learning community (Blanc et al. 2020, Li et al., 2021).'

Agreement on motivation from recent literature (C21-C23). Both evaluations accept this contextualization. OpenEval finds the inference in C23 follows logically from cited observations, while peer reviewers accept the positioning that the work challenges the 'steady state null drift' viewpoint without question.

Agreement on contextualization relative to prior work (C90-C91). Both evaluations accept this framing. OpenEval finds the characterization accurate though C92-C93 are somewhat speculative, while peer reviewers accept the positioning without challenge, noting the authors 'aim to challenge the latter viewpoint.'

Agreement on representational drift background (C1, C14, C15). Both evaluations accept this as appropriate context. OpenEval finds these well-established observations with appropriate citations, while peer reviewers accept the background framing, stating 'there is enough interest in this topic to justify the development of theoretical models of drift.'

Agreement on neuroscience background (C11-C13). Both evaluations accept these as well-established findings. OpenEval notes these are supported by classic citations (O'Keefe, Hubel & Wiesel, McNaughton), while peer reviewers accept the literature review without challenge.

Agreement on prior work context (C24-C26). Both evaluations accept this as accurate description of Qin et al., 2023. OpenEval finds this provides important context for extending to directed drift, while peer reviewers accept the background framing as part of the overall literature review.

Agreement on hypothesis background (C16-C20). Both evaluations accept this as appropriate literature summary. OpenEval finds these accurately summarize existing hypotheses with appropriate citations, while peer reviewers accept the theoretical landscape framing without question.

Agreement on main findings summary (C85-C87). Both evaluations accept these conclusions as well-supported. OpenEval notes appropriate caveats about generalization, while peer reviewers accept the mechanistic explanation as 'clearly laid out and convincing.'

Agreement on differential effects of noise types (C84, C109, C110). Both evaluations accept this as supported by theory and data. OpenEval notes consistency with Blanc et al., 2020 predictions, while peer reviewers accept the theoretical framework connecting noise type to regularization, noting it 'provides another set of tools for the neuroscience community.'

Agreement on theoretical predictions about noise (C98-C100). Both evaluations accept C98-C99 as well-supported. OpenEval notes C100 is speculative but follows logically, while peer reviewers accept this as generating 'testable hypotheses to examine in real neural data.'

Agreement on speculation about why other studies missed effects (C48, C74). Both evaluations accept these as reasonable speculation. OpenEval explicitly notes these are speculative, while peer reviewers accept them as part of the framework suggesting 'stationarity may be the hallmark of overfamiliarized environments.'

OpenEval evaluated claims about natural environments (C94-C95) as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct empirical support, representing future work rather than demonstrated results. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific speculative claims.

OpenEval found methodological caveats about interpretation of representational drift (C96-C97) to be SUPPORTED with appropriate citation (Brette, 2019). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these methodological points.

OpenEval evaluated implications for remapping (C101-C104) as UNCERTAIN, noting C101-C102 make reasonable points but C103 is speculative and C104 simply cites theory without testing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these remapping implications.

OpenEval found broader significance discussion (C105-C108) to be SUPPORTED, noting accurate characterization of novelty and valid general points about using ML theory for neuroscience. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these meta-level claims about the work's significance.
